overviewHtml:
This graded quiz assesses your understanding of how the problems of phenomenology took shape before Husserl. You'll be asked about Descartes's method of doubt and Kant's distinction between phenomena and things in themselves, Brentano's thesis of intentionality and his students' responses, and the differences among introspective psychology, causal explanation, and phenomenological description.

Note: Aim for a score of 80 percent or higher. If you score lower, use the feedback to review the topics you missed, then retake the quiz.

forms.stemHtml: What is the purpose of Descartes's method of doubt?

options.html: To prove that the external world doesn't exist
options.text: To prove that the external world doesn't exist
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Descartes's method of doubt.

options.html: To find what's certain by setting aside all doubtful beliefs
options.text: To find what's certain by setting aside all doubtful beliefs
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Descartes uses doubt as a filter. He sets aside any belief that admits even slight doubt, so that only what's certain gets through.

options.html: To show that the senses are always mistaken about everything
options.text: To show that the senses are always mistaken about everything
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Descartes's method of doubt.

options.html: To replace philosophy with experimental natural science
options.text: To replace philosophy with experimental natural science
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Descartes's method of doubt.

forms.stemHtml: In the wax example, why does Descartes conclude that the wax is grasped by the mind alone?

options.html: Every sensible quality changes near the fire, yet the same wax remains
options.text: Every sensible quality changes near the fire, yet the same wax remains
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Because no sensible quality stays the same while the wax does, the wax's identity can't come from the senses. Descartes concludes that it's grasped by the mind.

options.html: The wax has no sensible qualities before it's brought near the fire
options.text: The wax has no sensible qualities before it's brought near the fire
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Descartes and perception as judgment.

options.html: The senses report the wax's changes accurately and completely
options.text: The senses report the wax's changes accurately and completely
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Descartes and perception as judgment.

options.html: Imagination pictures every possible shape the wax could take
options.text: Imagination pictures every possible shape the wax could take
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Descartes and perception as judgment.

forms.stemHtml: For Kant, what can be known?

options.html: Things as they are in themselves, apart from any experience
options.text: Things as they are in themselves, apart from any experience
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Kant's Copernican turn.

options.html: Phenomena, objects as they appear to us in experience
options.text: Phenomena, objects as they appear to us in experience
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Knowledge reaches as far as possible experience. Phenomena can be known. Things in themselves can be thought but not known.

options.html: Only one's own existence as a thinking thing
options.text: Only one's own existence as a thinking thing
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Kant's Copernican turn.

options.html: Only objects that science has measured directly
options.text: Only objects that science has measured directly
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Kant's Copernican turn.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following does Kant treat as forms of intuition? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: Space

options.html: Causality
options.text: Causality
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Kant's Copernican turn.

options.html: Time

options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Time is the form of inner sense.

options.html: Substance
options.text: Substance
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Kant's Copernican turn.

forms.stemHtml: Complete Brentano's term for the way every mental act contains an object: intentional ________.

options.html: inexistence
options.text: inexistence
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Intentional inexistence is the object's existence "in" the act as its object, whether or not it exists outside the act.

options.html: nonexistence
options.text: nonexistence
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Brentano's intentional inexistence.

options.html: existence
options.text: existence
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Brentano's intentional inexistence.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Brentano's intentional inexistence.

forms.stemHtml: Which experience is most often cited against the claim that every mental phenomenon is directed at an object?

options.html: Judging that it will rain heavily tomorrow afternoon
options.text: Judging that it will rain heavily tomorrow afternoon
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on intentionality as the mark of the mental.

options.html: A diffuse anxiety that isn't about anything in particular
options.text: A diffuse anxiety that isn't about anything in particular
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Moods like diffuse anxiety don't seem to be directed at any object. That makes them the standard challenge to the necessity claim.

options.html: Remembering a long conversation from yesterday evening
options.text: Remembering a long conversation from yesterday evening
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on intentionality as the mark of the mental.

options.html: Wanting a strong cup of coffee right after a long lunch
options.text: Wanting a strong cup of coffee right after a long lunch
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on intentionality as the mark of the mental.

forms.stemHtml: How does Twardowski distinguish the content of a presentation from its object?

options.html: The content is a physical thing, and the object is its mental image
options.text: The content is a physical thing, and the object is its mental image
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Twardowski's content–object distinction.

options.html: The content exists in the mind with the act, and the object may not exist
options.text: The content exists in the mind with the act, and the object may not exist
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The content is the mental item through which the act is directed. The object is what the presentation is of, and it may not exist.

options.html: The content is what is judged, and the object is what is loved
options.text: The content is what is judged, and the object is what is loved
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Twardowski's content–object distinction.

options.html: The content and the object are one entity under two names
options.text: The content and the object are one entity under two names
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Twardowski's content–object distinction.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following statements are phenomenological descriptions? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: "The phrase unfolded as one whole, each note heard against the notes just past."
options.text: "The phrase unfolded as one whole, each note heard against the notes just past."
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! This describes how the melody was given in experience, as an unfolding whole.

options.html: "Pressure waves stimulated the cochlea and auditory nerve."
options.text: "Pressure waves stimulated the cochlea and auditory nerve."
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on causal explanation and phenomenological description.

options.html: "The next note was expected before it sounded."
options.text: "The next note was expected before it sounded."
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! This describes how the melody was given, including the anticipation of what comes next.

options.html: "I had a sequence of auditory sensations of varying pitch."
options.text: "I had a sequence of auditory sensations of varying pitch."
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on causal explanation and phenomenological description.

forms.stemHtml: What was the name of Titchener's program of analyzing consciousness into its elementary processes, the way anatomy analyzes the body?

options.html: structuralism
options.text: structuralism
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Titchener's structuralism asked what the mind's elements are and how they're arranged.

options.html: structural psychology
options.text: structural psychology
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Titchener's structural psychology, or structuralism, asked what the mind's elements are and how they're arranged.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Wundt, Titchener, and introspective psychology.

forms.stemHtml: Why did the imageless-thought controversy damage introspective psychology?

options.html: It showed that laboratory equipment distorted observers' reports
options.text: It showed that laboratory equipment distorted observers' reports
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Wundt, Titchener, and introspective psychology.

options.html: Trained observers disagreed, and introspection couldn't settle it
options.text: Trained observers disagreed, and introspection couldn't settle it
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Würzburg and Titchener's observers reported different findings about thought, and introspection offered no independent way to decide between them.

options.html: It proved that all thinking consists of vivid mental images
options.text: It proved that all thinking consists of vivid mental images
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Wundt, Titchener, and introspective psychology.

options.html: It proved that thinking has no conscious features whatsoever
options.text: It proved that thinking has no conscious features whatsoever
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Wundt, Titchener, and introspective psychology.

forms.stemHtml: In the First Meditation, Descartes supposes a powerful, malicious deceiver. What does this supposition accomplish?

options.html: It proves that God exists and so guarantees all knowledge
options.text: It proves that God exists and so guarantees all knowledge
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Descartes's method of doubt.

options.html: It shows that dreams arise from bodily causes during sleep
options.text: It shows that dreams arise from bodily causes during sleep
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Descartes's method of doubt.

options.html: It extends doubt to beliefs that survived the dream argument
options.text: It extends doubt to beliefs that survived the dream argument
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Simple truths of arithmetic seem to survive the dream argument. The deceiver supposition extends doubt even to these.

options.html: It establishes that his own body certainly exists after all
options.text: It establishes that his own body certainly exists after all
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Descartes's method of doubt.

forms.stemHtml: Descartes says that from his window he sees only hats and coats, yet he judges that people are passing. What does this example illustrate?

options.html: That the senses give perfectly reliable knowledge of people
options.text: That the senses give perfectly reliable knowledge of people
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Descartes and perception as judgment.

options.html: That other people don't really exist beneath their clothing
options.text: That other people don't really exist beneath their clothing
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Descartes and perception as judgment.

options.html: That perceiving a thing involves a judgment beyond the senses
options.text: That perceiving a thing involves a judgment beyond the senses
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The example extends the wax point. The unity or identity of what's perceived is supplied by the mind's judgment, not by the senses alone.

options.html: That imagination supplies the images of passing people
options.text: That imagination supplies the images of passing people
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Descartes and perception as judgment.

forms.stemHtml: A researcher claims that atoms are the thing in itself, which physics will eventually reveal. How would Kant respond?

options.html: He would agree, because physics studies things in themselves
options.text: He would agree, because physics studies things in themselves
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Kant's Copernican turn.

options.html: He would agree, because atoms can't be seen with the senses
options.text: He would agree, because atoms can't be seen with the senses
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Kant's Copernican turn.

options.html: He would object, because atoms are mere illusions
options.text: He would object, because atoms are mere illusions
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Kant's Copernican turn.

options.html: He would object, because science studies only phenomena
options.text: He would object, because science studies only phenomena
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Science studies phenomena, so its findings stay on the side of appearance. The thing in itself isn't a hidden physical object for science to find.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following are among Kant's categories, the pure concepts of the understanding? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: Space
options.text: Space
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Kant's Copernican turn.

options.html: Substance
options.text: Substance
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Substance is one of the categories. It lets experience present an enduring thing.

options.html: Causality
options.text: Causality
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Causality is one of the categories. It lets experience present changes as having causes.

options.html: Time
options.text: Time
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Kant's Copernican turn.

forms.stemHtml: In Brentano's classification, what is the basic class of mental acts, on which every other act is based? Enter a single word.

options.html: presentation
options.text: presentation
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Presentation is having something before the mind at all. Judgments and phenomena of love and hate are based on presentations.

options.html: presentations
options.text: presentations
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Presentation is having something before the mind at all. Judgments and phenomena of love and hate are based on presentations.

options.html: judgment
options.text: judgment
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Brentano's three classes of mental acts.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Brentano's three classes of mental acts.

forms.stemHtml: How do some defenders of Brentano's thesis respond to the case of moods?

options.html: They argue that moods aren't mental phenomena at all
options.text: They argue that moods aren't mental phenomena at all
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on intentionality as the mark of the mental.

options.html: They argue that moods are physical phenomena, like colors
options.text: They argue that moods are physical phenomena, like colors
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on intentionality as the mark of the mental.

options.html: They argue that moods are directed at the world as a whole
options.text: They argue that moods are directed at the world as a whole
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! On this reinterpretation, a mood has an object after all: the world as a whole, rather than any one thing in it. Critics reply that this stretches "directedness" too far.

options.html: They argue that moods are judgments about oneself
options.text: They argue that moods are judgments about oneself
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on intentionality as the mark of the mental.

forms.stemHtml: What principle underlies Meinong's theory of objects?

options.html: An object exists if and only if someone presents it
options.text: An object exists if and only if someone presents it
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Meinong's theory of objects.

options.html: Only objects that exist can have any properties
options.text: Only objects that exist can have any properties
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Meinong's theory of objects.

options.html: What an object is like is independent of whether it exists
options.text: What an object is like is independent of whether it exists
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Meinong's principle is the independence of being-so (Sosein) from being (Sein), which is why a golden mountain can be golden without existing.

options.html: Every object exists inside the mental act as its content
options.text: Every object exists inside the mental act as its content
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Meinong's theory of objects.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following statements about seeing an apple are causal explanations? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: "Long-wavelength light reflected from the apple's surface."
options.text: "Long-wavelength light reflected from the apple's surface."
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! This names a physical cause of the experience.

options.html: "The apple's back side was given as there, though unseen."
options.text: "The apple's back side was given as there, though unseen."
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading comparing three ways of studying experience.

options.html: "Retinal cones responded, and the visual cortex processed the color."
options.text: "Retinal cones responded, and the visual cortex processed the color."
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! This names physiological causes of the experience.

options.html: "I had a patch of red sensation and a mild pleasant feeling."
options.text: "I had a patch of red sensation and a mild pleasant feeling."
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading comparing three ways of studying experience.

forms.stemHtml: What was Titchener's two-word term for reporting the object that causes an experience rather than the experience's elementary processes?

options.html: stimulus error
options.text: stimulus error
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Titchener's trained observers were to report sensations and feelings, not the object, such as "an apple," that caused them.

options.html: the stimulus error
options.text: the stimulus error
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Titchener's trained observers were to report sensations and feelings, not the object that caused them.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Wundt, Titchener, and introspective psychology.

forms.stemHtml: How does Dilthey's descriptive psychology differ from explanatory psychology?

options.html: It measures mental processes with laboratory instruments
options.text: It measures mental processes with laboratory instruments
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Dilthey's explaining and understanding.

options.html: It starts from the lived connectedness of mental life and describes it
options.text: It starts from the lived connectedness of mental life and describes it
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Explanatory psychology derives mental life from hypothetical elements and causal laws. Dilthey's descriptive psychology starts from mental life as a lived whole and describes and analyzes it.

options.html: It derives mental life from hypothetical elements and causal laws
options.text: It derives mental life from hypothetical elements and causal laws
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Dilthey's explaining and understanding.

options.html: It reduces mental life to physiological processes in the brain
options.text: It reduces mental life to physiological processes in the brain
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Dilthey's explaining and understanding.

forms.stemHtml: Why does "I am, I exist" survive Descartes's doubt?

options.html: Because the senses reliably confirm that one's body exists
options.text: Because the senses reliably confirm that one's body exists
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Descartes's method of doubt and the cogito.

options.html: Because simple truths of arithmetic hold even in dreams
options.text: Because simple truths of arithmetic hold even in dreams
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Descartes's method of doubt and the cogito.

options.html: Because God guarantees that simple beliefs are true
options.text: Because God guarantees that simple beliefs are true
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Descartes's method of doubt and the cogito.

options.html: Because being deceived requires a thinker who exists
options.text: Because being deceived requires a thinker who exists
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! However powerful the deceiver, it can't make Descartes nothing while he thinks. So "I am, I exist" is true whenever he thinks it.

forms.stemHtml: On Descartes's account, why can't imagination grasp the wax?

options.html: Imagination works only on objects that are absent from view
options.text: Imagination works only on objects that are absent from view
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Descartes and perception as judgment.

options.html: The wax can take more shapes than imagination could run through
options.text: The wax can take more shapes than imagination could run through
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! What remains of the wax is something extended, flexible, and changeable. It can take more shapes than imagination could ever picture, so imagination can't be what grasps it.

options.html: Imagination is a kind of bodily sensation, not a mental act
options.text: Imagination is a kind of bodily sensation, not a mental act
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Descartes and perception as judgment.

options.html: The wax has no shape at all once it has melted completely
options.text: The wax has no shape at all once it has melted completely
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Descartes and perception as judgment.

forms.stemHtml: Kant calls the concept of a noumenon a boundary concept. What does that mean?

options.html: It names the physical edge of the observable universe
options.text: It names the physical edge of the observable universe
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Kant's thing in itself.

options.html: It marks the limit of what sensibility can claim
options.text: It marks the limit of what sensibility can claim
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The concept's role is to limit the claims of sensibility, marking that what appears isn't everything that can be thought.

options.html: It names the line between mind and body
options.text: It names the line between mind and body
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Kant's thing in itself.

options.html: It marks where space ends and time begins
options.text: It marks where space ends and time begins

forms.stemHtml: Kant holds that space and time are empirically real and transcendentally ideal. Which statements follow? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: Space and time hold of everything we can experience
options.text: Space and time hold of everything we can experience
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! This is what "empirically real" means.

options.html: Space and time are nothing apart from the conditions of sensibility
options.text: Space and time are nothing apart from the conditions of sensibility
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! This is what "transcendentally ideal" means.

options.html: Space and time are learned by generalizing from experience
options.text: Space and time are learned by generalizing from experience
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Kant's Copernican turn.

options.html: Space and time are properties of things in themselves
options.text: Space and time are properties of things in themselves
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Kant's Copernican turn.

forms.stemHtml: Complete the name of Brentano's proposal that intentionality belongs to all and only mental phenomena: the mark-of-the-________ thesis.

options.html: mental
options.text: mental
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The mark-of-the-mental thesis holds that directedness toward an object is what separates mental phenomena from physical ones.

options.html: mind
options.text: mind
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on intentionality as the mark of the mental.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on intentionality as the mark of the mental.

forms.stemHtml: The mark-of-the-mental thesis makes a sufficiency claim. What does that claim say?

options.html: Whatever is mental is directed at an object
options.text: Whatever is mental is directed at an object
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on intentionality as the mark of the mental.

options.html: Whatever is directed at an object is mental
options.text: Whatever is directed at an object is mental
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The sufficiency claim says directedness is enough to make something mental. This is why questions about whether a machine's states are genuinely about anything bear on whether it has mental states.

options.html: Whatever is physical is directed at nothing
options.text: Whatever is physical is directed at nothing
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on intentionality as the mark of the mental.

options.html: Whatever is presented is also judged
options.text: Whatever is presented is also judged
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on intentionality as the mark of the mental.

forms.stemHtml: When you present the god Jupiter, what is your act directed at, according to Husserl?

options.html: A mental image of Jupiter stored inside consciousness
options.text: A mental image of Jupiter stored inside consciousness
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Husserl's objection to immanent objects.

options.html: Nothing, since Jupiter doesn't exist
options.text: Nothing, since Jupiter doesn't exist
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Husserl's objection to immanent objects.

options.html: A nonexistent object that has being-so but no being
options.text: A nonexistent object that has being-so but no being
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Husserl's objection to immanent objects.

options.html: Jupiter himself, the god of myth, whether or not he exists
options.text: Jupiter himself, the god of myth, whether or not he exists
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Husserl denies that the object is a mental item inside consciousness. The act is directed at Jupiter himself, and no component of the experience is a mental Jupiter.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following statements about anxiety before a talk are introspective reports? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: "I felt tension in my chest and heat in my face."
options.text: "I felt tension in my chest and heat in my face."

options.html: "The audience showed up as a group about to judge."
options.text: "The audience showed up as a group about to judge."

options.html: "I had an unpleasant feeling of moderate intensity."
options.text: "I had an unpleasant feeling of moderate intensity."

options.html: "A stress response raised my heart rate."
options.text: "A stress response raised my heart rate."

forms.stemHtml: Brentano held that we have inner perception of our present mental states, but not inner ________ of them. Enter one word.

options.html: observation
options.text: observation
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! For Brentano, attending to a present mental state as an object disturbs it, so inner observation is possible only in memory.

options.html: perception
options.text: perception
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on causal explanation and phenomenological description.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on causal explanation and phenomenological description.

options.html: It relied on untrained volunteers reporting whatever they noticed
options.text: It relied on untrained volunteers reporting whatever they noticed

options.text: It studied higher thought processes such as reasoning in full detail
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Review the reading on Wundt, Titchener, and introspective psychology.

options.text: It used controlled conditions with systematically varied stimuli
